utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. If the witness could be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Peko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'll remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic: [Continued].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Peko. I'm going to try and ask you some more questions. I hope I'll be shorter than I said I would be yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher -- [In English] Visual contact with the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Peko, just tell me briefly, please, whether anybody edited or redacted the minutes and notes that you compiled.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody change anything in your notes on the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are all the reports, or rather, all the notes, did all the notes make up the preliminary report in the way that you told us about and as you handed them over to the institute?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the authors of the preliminary report, or any advisors that were used in compiling the report, did they look through or edit any of your notes?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day before yesterday, if I'm right, you mentioned a shell that fell in Boskoviceva Street on the 23rd of October; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when that was, exactly?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd of October, but I don't know the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what house was damaged at the time?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the houses in the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the number of the house, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Boskoviceva number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that looking at it from the plats is it on the left or right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, were any other houses, surrounding houses, damaged?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me which ones?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house opposite Boskoviceva, the roofs to the houses opposite, and the synagogue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what street the synagogue is in?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The synagogue is in Zudioska Street, but the structure has a facade facing Boskoviceva and the other street too, Rudevska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, to look through some notes. May I ask the usher to show the witness the first binder of the exhibit, that is to say, of the preliminary report that we have already looked at. We looked at it yesterday, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like, madam, to ask you to take a look at insula 6, structure 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Your Honours, that is the ERN B/C/S number 01069396 for the B/C/S version, and the English translation is at L0061066.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you found the page number?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 396, the last digits?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Take a look now, please, at this piece of information, the date when the building was hit. Does it say the 6th of December, 1991 there?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me why it wasn't necessary to say that the structure was hit on the 21st of October, 1991 -- the 23rd of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness gives her answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I would beg a certain amount of caution with respect to this question since the witness said I think it was the 3rd of -- 23rd -- sorry, it was number 3 Boskoviceva Street which was hit. She didn't say outright that she knew it was number 3 Boskoviceva Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I did not compile the report, and I can't find my way around it now. Now, the projectile that fell on the facade of that particular structure damaged structure 1 and structure 2, and the structures on the opposite side of the street as well, and they are structures in a series of structures. I did not draw up the actual list, and I don't know the actual place of damage, but I do know that an alcove was damaged in Boskoviceva number 3. I would have to look at all this in detail to be able to see where it actually was, and I can't be held responsible for reports on these structures, I just know that the impressions I gained from the first impact that struck that particular street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm not asking you about those reports. I'm just asking you whether you might perhaps know why all the dates weren't listed, why the only date is the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that the report records all the damage done up until the 6th of December, so it's very difficult, or rather, not even necessary to go into when what damage was caused. Now, I can't actually say now why it was written the way it was. Perhaps it was omitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like you to take a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I take a moment to consult, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't be needing the binder any more. We've finished with it. Can you tell me, please, whether, in the months of October, November, December 1991, did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the general alarm was not sounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the headquarters, or rather, the offices of your company called Arhitekt is?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gunduliceva Poljana number 6, also in Dubrovnik in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Now, at that time, or during that time, did you leave the Old Town at all when the alarm was not sounded?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely, because my parents lived in Gruz, for example, and I couldn't see them for three months. But yes, I went to visit two of my elderly aunts, so I would go to the Placa area, where we had to wait in line for food. In October, we had no food, for example. There was no food in the shops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me where your aunts lived.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area of Ilijina Glavica, and it's in the region of the summer houses of Skocibuha. Boninovo is the general area. Ilijina Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Glavica is the more specific term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it near Valtazar Bogisic Street?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where that street is exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the part of town which we link to Bogisic Park, for example, that general area?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's quite a lot further. The other one is Vladimir Nazor Street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In the statement you gave to the investigators on the 4th of July, 2000, you mentioned that you had heard that the Croatian forces had some cannons. Is that right? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just one sentence in my statement, in a lengthier paragraph. What I was saying generally was that there were no weapons, I never saw any weapons. Moreover, as an example, I said that we heard that there were some weapons that were out of use, that couldn't be used. Now, the way in which this was formulated wasn't the happiest solution, but I didn't want to intervene. But what I wanted to say is this: In the shelters, people would talk about aid and assistance daily that would be coming in to us, that would be arriving. And the stories that went around the shelters in most cases were geared towards debating whether we would be getting any aid and assistance or not. So this was one of the stories that was going around. There were different stories going around, and the worst thing was to hear that there was something couldn't be used, that was useless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, of those 90 days in October, November, and December, how much time did you actually spend in a shelter?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of October, when I was still residing in my apartment in Zlatni Potok, we would spend part of the day in the shelter, when you could hear the explosions going off. So I can't tell you exactly how much time. In November, we also spent five days, or rather, we were in the shelter all the time, lying down on the floor. Otherwise, we would move around the apartment cautiously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's try and get through this as fast as possible. How many days, was my question; five, six, seven? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't count the days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we had two days in October and four days in November and one day in December, how many days is that altogether?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't put it that way. We were very often taking shelter in the premises we were in anyway. It's like this: If you hear something hitting a roof and the roof reverberates, and you have the feeling that it was a bullet, you won't be up in the attic area; you would be down in the bottom of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what was your experience in that way?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in the building in Prijeko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So a bullet hit the roof; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a case like that, and you have to do what you can. The important thing was to survive and to protect yourself, and so we spent a long time in the shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did the bullet cause any damage, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Once again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: As I remarked yesterday, just for the sake of consistency, the word "bullet," I would like to check for the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter says today it is "bullet."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This time I used the word "bullet" as opposed to the word "shell," so I can confirm that and I'm sure the interpretation booths can confirm that too, Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who you heard about the cannons from?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps hear where those cannons were located?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see when you went to visit your aunt at Ilijina Glavica, did you happen to see a mortar there, perhaps, or mortars?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you yesterday that I couldn't recognise a mortar but that I didn't see any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any weapons at all at Ilijina Glavica?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any people, soldiers, civilians, anybody round about that was engaged in some sort of defence business around Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that those cannons were not completely operational. Now, could you tell me how you know that?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was within the frameworks of the same piece of news. Something -- as far as I'm concerned, something either works or doesn't work. So weapons are not decorative objects, for them to be able to function partially or be partially operational. They either work or they don't work. So these were cannons -- well, I don't know if it was cannons or guns or some other type of weapon. I don't know the exact term that should be applied to them. But anyway, I quoted this as an example. Yes, I did hear things like that, but I heard people say that it was useless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the Croatian artillery firing in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear whether the Croatian army or Croatian defence forces opened fire from the area of Dubrovnik at all?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say "the town of Dubrovnik," I'm not -- I don't mean the Old Town nucleus only; I mean the Old Town, I mean Gruz and Lapad and Boninovo, and the eastern part of town. Did you ever hear anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you, I was mostly in the old part of town, and no, we didn't discuss things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interested in knowing whether your town had any defence mechanisms from the attackers?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we were interested in that. However, at the very beginning, at the outset, we already knew that people were spontaneously rising up to organise a defence for the town and were, of course, being killed. That's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you know about that? Who were the people who rose up? Who were the people who were killed?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of October, when the five of us - my husband, his mother, that is to say, my mother-in-law, and his stepfather; then there was Mrs. Jelena Milisic and I myself - when we arrived in town, she arrived as a widow and we arrived to the building in which there was a young woman with two children, she was a widow too, and her husband was killed in the Zupa Dubravacka defending his own house. So I found myself faced with this situation at the very outset. I had this unpleasant opportunity of becoming confronted with two individuals who were in deep mourning, couldn't believe what was happening to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. In your statement, you also say that some local men carried their personal, privately owned weapons when they performed security duties within the Old Town. Is that what you actually said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that because I know that my husband, for instance, on one occasion, was at a place within the Dubrovnik lazarets in order to control what was going on, for security reasons. Because from the 1st of October, there was a ban on movements, or rather, a curfew from 9.00 in the evening to the morning. So you weren't allowed to move about. But in the evening, nonetheless, groups of people did organise themselves to control and supervise and see what was going on. And the gentleman who was with him had a hunting rifle, and he had --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think the witness said a weapon too. Could Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. she repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was within the frameworks of the civilian defence system. There was no commanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that how it was all through those three months or did the situation change?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was once. I don't know what the date was. I think it was sometime in November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your husband a military conscript?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said here some of the local men did carry their personal privately owned weapons when they performed security duties within the Old Town, you actually meant only your husband?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My husband told me about this, and there was a man with him. There was two of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any units of the Croatian army in the town of Dubrovnik, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anybody who was in the units of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. The Croatian army actually came into being later as a firmer organisation. I mean, I don't know about these things, and I don't really think about it very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see soldiers in uniform at Stradun or somewhere else in the Old Town, soldiers of the Croatian army in uniform in Stradun in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, at that time it wasn't the Croatian army during those first months. Perhaps these were just men who were wearing some kind of olive-grey clothing. But no, really, I never saw any of them armed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about military-aged men? Were they allowed to leave town?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that men from the ages of 16 to 60 were not allowed to leave town, regardless of whether they were able-bodied or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why? We have not recorded an answer. Could you just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your house in Zlatni Potok? Was it damaged?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any positions, defence positions of the Croatian army in the immediate vicinity of your house?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave this statement to the investigator on the 4th of July, 2000, and you said that you gave these preliminary reports that we talked about over the past two or three days to the investigator; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. Can I add something in response to your question, your previous question? You just asked me about Zlatni Potok, but my husband's house and his mother's house was completely burned down. That was in another area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We heard about that. But let's go back to the two questions I still have. When you spoke to the investigator, it was Mr. Michael Stephens, if I'm not mistaken, you handed over to him this preliminary report that we're discussing here?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you gave him this report, you signed it as well?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is what I was asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just ask one more time, the very last time - and I do apologise to the Trial Chamber and everybody else - just one more time, could we have the second binder shown to the witness, please. The second binder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at page 01069596. And in English it is 0061482. Is that the report that you gave to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: 596 are the last digits; right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you signed that statement on the 4th of July, 2000; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see Mr. Vetma's signature here?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the date by the signature?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How come Mr. Vetma's signature is on the copy that you handed over to the investigator?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. As far as this building is concerned, and I believe many others as well, we, as a three-member commission, toured these buildings, and I see no reason why there would not be three signatures on one page of the people who took part in this. You don't think that there should be three separate pages, do you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But please explain this to me. If you gave this report to the investigator on the 4th of July, 2000, and if Mr. Vetma signed it on the 30th of June - that's what it says here - how come the signature is there? Did you take it to him to sign it?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That means that Mr. Vetma gave a similar statement on the 30th of July and that I gave a statement on the 4th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 30th of June, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So from the report, individual reports were taken. So if this was shown to me on the 4th of July and if it was shown to Mr. Vetma on the 30th of June, I don't see that there's any problem. Well, you see, I do not keep these reports in my bureau or in my house, so the reports are at the Cultural Monuments Protection Institute. So it is officials from the institute who brought these reports in. These are pages that have to do with my statement. They were taken out, and then I assume they were put back in to this entire set of documents at the time of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not hand over the report to the investigator, that he already had it?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, all the papers that have to do with my statement were in one place, and it is only natural that I signed them. These are reports about buildings that I worked on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who prepared it? If you did not hand over the report, who did? And why did you tell me a short while ago that you gave him the report if you were not the one who gave him the report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, he asked for signatures on the forms that had to do with the damage sustained by individual buildings that I worked on. Now, who gave who what, I think is of no relevance. But this was the set of documents that this section was taken out of, the one that had to do with my own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just one more question. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what damage was sustained by the Orthodox Church in Dubrovnik? Is it true that it was destroyed, the Orthodox Church in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have something by way of clarification that has to do with the questions I put yesterday. It has to do with something that happened at 13.53, or rather, 13 hours, 0 minutes, 53 seconds, according to the transcript. That is the situation when Mrs. Vetma -- I'm sorry, Mrs. Peko - sorry - said that perhaps I, as the Defence attorney, know who was firing from Srdj. But the transcript says that it was an insult addressed to Mr. Strugar. This was an insult addressed to the Defence of Mr. Strugar. I was informed by the interpreters yesterday that this was a mistake, and also Mrs. Peko at that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. point said that she apologised to me for what I said -- rather, what she said, that she said that I was shooting from there maybe. So I accept her apology, of course, and I understand that it happened in the heat of the debate that we were conducting yesterday. That is the only thing I wish to add in this context, and I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Petrovic. The Chamber felt that there was some misunderstanding in the heat of the moment, and I'm glad you acknowledge that. Yes. Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Re-examined by Mr. Kaufman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Peko, only a few more questions. Now, in cross-examination you were questioned about the 6th of December, and you told the Trial Chamber that your husband had assumed that the projectile which hit the house in which you were a resident on that day was a guided rocket. Those are the words that appeared in the transcript. Do you know what a guided rocket is?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I assume that it can be guided precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a guided rocket in the course of your work on those days?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. But I saw these white traces that are allegedly used for guiding rockets. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean by "white traces"?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that four buildings were completely burned down, and you didn't have an opportunity to tell the Trial Chamber which those buildings were, although you wanted to. I now offer you that opportunity. Please tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that nine buildings in Dubrovnik were completely destroyed in the fire. That is to say, they were hit by incendiary projectiles and therefore destroyed. They burned down. I had the opportunity of monitoring, as an architect, four buildings. For two buildings, I made the complete project documentation, so I was familiarised in detail with the damage sustained by these buildings. I also worked on other buildings that were not totally destroyed in town, and I can tell you exactly which ones those were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps for the sake of time alone, if you remember the names of those four buildings in the Old Town upon which you worked and which were completely burned down.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did this architectural monitoring for the street in Sigurate number 2, that's the address. Then Od Puca number 16, then the building in Siroka Street number 5, and the building in Miha Pracata number 6. These houses were completely destroyed, but the building in Siroka number 5 is actually part of a larger block which is called the Maineri Djordjic palace. I also worked on the Sorkocevic palace by Gunduliceva Poljana. I think the street is Zeljarica number 5. And the Ranjina palace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at one point in your testimony, Ms. Peko, you talked about a thousand shells falling on the Old Town on the 6th of December. And when you were talking about insula number 11, you said that this was examined but damaged in a minor way. Those were the words that appeared in the transcript yesterday. If that was damaged in a minor way, according to you, insula number 11, where was the major damage on that day?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The major damage was sustained, and you will see it on the map if you have a look at it, by the central part of town. That is in parts of the main street, Placa, then the blocks of buildings on the southern side and on the northern side. From the east to the west, looking at the city walls. That is the part of town that was affected more badly. For example, the area of Pustijerna, or Karmen as we call it within town, was the one that was damaged the least perhaps. But the central part of town was affected very badly. I must say that it is in that part of town that there is a major concentration of valuable buildings like Baroque palaces and churches and monasteries like the Dominican monastery and the church of St. Vlaho and the Church of Our Savior that we already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But of course, the damage was not just confined to that particular area of the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. But that is where the projectiles fell with greater frequency. Of course there was damage wherever projectiles fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, two more questions, Ms. Peko. The first concerns the examination -- cross-examination that was made on the point of the editing of your notes, or the lack of editing thereof. Now, you said that after you submitted your report, none of the authors edited or looked through your notes. Now, I'd like you to clarify that, perhaps. What happened after you finished that report on a particular site that you had been examining?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: After compiling a report, I would hand it over for it to be typed out, and then I would check it once again before it would be binded together. It is only natural that the authors of the entire project should have insight into the material that they are putting together, and ultimately, they take part in drafting the map that has to do with pinpointing the damage and categorising the damage. Of course they're involved in this work throughout. But it was my understanding that the question put to me was whether somebody edited the text that I had actually written, and that is why I said no, nobody changed the text that I wrote. As for the report as a whole, there were just two words I really wanted to say in addition to what I've already said already, so may I? The preliminary report of course means that it is preliminary, that it precedes something, at the moment when the most information can be received about the damaged buildings. Immediately after this period, work had already started on the affected buildings in order to prevent the rain from harming them any further, in order to make life in these buildings possible, and so on and so forth. I would like to repeat once again that emphasis is laid on the damage sustained by the building. I myself was personally most interested in the degree of damage sustained by the buildings. I personally found it hard sometimes when I had to write down that there was a lesser degree of damage on a particularly valuable building, but that's the way it had to be done, and it had to be evaluated in such a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Peko, I thank you for that clarification, because it was not clear from the way it was answered in cross-examination. Now, the final matter which I want to turn to is the questions that you were asked concerning the San Franciscan Monastery, and the preponderance of impacts in the cloister of that San Franciscan Monastery. If I may remind you, you were asked about the preponderance of impacts which occurred in the southwestern corner of that cloister, and then you were asked about the direction of fire. And you, using your architectural abilities, stated that it came from the east. You were then cross-examined, and it was put to you that you knew that because you had seen the JNA in the east to north-east. Now, continuing that particular vein, I would like to ask Ms. Usher if she could place in front of you the first bundle and the page numbered 01069074 in the B/C/S version. This is a diagram.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness. We're sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have page 01069074 in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does this portray? Perhaps you could enlighten us.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the map of the town, with damage sustained by the city walls. Because I see that that has been marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at that, could you tell us which side of the walls was damaged? The inside or the outside?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this question, for two reasons at least. One reason is that I did not open this subject at all in my questions regarding the preliminary report. Secondly, the lady, the witness, did not work on this at all, this portion that is being shown. She did not even mention the city walls in her report. The third reason is that, from the map, one cannot see the points that are there. There is nothing on this map that can show whether it was one side of the wall or the other side of the wall. One would have to read the report in order to ascertain what actually happened. Otherwise, it would be impossible to tell. So those are the three reasons why I think that the question that my learned friend put should not be pursued any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am aware that the witness did not work on this particular site, but then my learned friend himself, in cross-examination, did put to the witness various sites, some of which the witness did not work, and even cross-examined her on them. I take, for example, the last item which was put to the witness in Boskoviceva Street number 3, L0061006. Once again, that was an item which the witness herself did not examine in the course of her duties for the protection of institutes -- the Institute for the Protection of Monuments, and yet she was cross-examined on the matter. I did not raise an objection apart from wishing to caution my learned friend as to the way in which he phrased the question. The third point is that -- if I may address the third point that Mr. Petrovic raised. There is a -- of course, a written record of this particular item and it is to be found in the English translation at L0061460. And if I may address the general thrust of my learned friend's objection, it is Mr. Petrovic himself who opened this line of questioning up in cross-examination when he tried to draw conclusions as to the trajectory from the preponderance of impacts, as I explained in the question, in the south-western corner of the cloister of the monastery, the Franciscan Monastery, not the San Franciscan Monastery as I said earlier, the Franciscan Monastery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You put it that Mr. Petrovic tried to draw conclusions. Was it not that he was questioning whether the witness could draw conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, and the witness did draw a conclusion. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to pursue the same line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How do we then move from that particular site - and the questioning, as I recall it, was confined to the issue of where the shell or shells may have come that caused that particular damage - how do we move from there in cross-examination to, for the first time, a consideration of the damage to the walls of the city in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Well, I moved to that by asking for a certain amount of liberty in the sites that I present to this witness, since Mr. Petrovic himself has allowed himself a certain amount of liberty in presenting sites and the Prosecution has not objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But I didn't understand the questioning in cross-examination to be at large about the source of the shelling but the point that was in issue in the point of cross-examination was the damage to one particular building and one part of that damage only. You are now seeking to have the witness deal with entirely different damage to other structures and with no apparent connection with the point that was being cross-examined. Have I misconstrued the situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I hear Your Honour's point, and I take it, and I shall not continue this line of questioning, and I shall continue it with Dr. Kaiser when he comes next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I could well see that that may be a consequence, but I think Mr. Petrovic's objection is well-founded at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour, and I thank Ms. Peko for coming to the Trial Chamber. I wonder if Your Honours have any questions of Ms. Peko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are two that occur to me, at least. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first: We had emphasised by you, Mrs. Peko, that this is a preliminary report. Was there a final report?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I don't work in the Institute for Protection. But of course it is normal in cases of that kind, as previously when a report was done on the earthquake, that more precise reports are compiled with an evaluation of the damage and possible recommendations for repairs and reconstruction. So that was a preliminary report. Later reports were of course far more detailed, and are always far more detailed. There are certainly no facts about weapons, and they will be able to be drawn up at a later stage. The first preliminary report gives an overview immediately after the events of what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. The second matter -- I was pausing. I thought interpretation was still carrying on, but apparently not. The second matter, both in cross-examination and in your evidence in chief and re-examination, one matter was mentioned. I remain unclear, I'm afraid, as to what you meant, and it may be that it is a matter of the way it's been put in the English language rather than in yours. It's this issue of white traces. Can you tell the Chamber what it is that you actually saw. Can you describe it.

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 7th of December, from the apartment we were in, I left the apartment and went out into the street, and as people had already started clearing up the streets, it was my wish to collect the stones that fell from our building which was hit, so that we could keep those old stones for future repairs and reconstruction. That's what I wanted to do. And when I was doing that, I saw some white -- the word "nit" means thread or strand. I think that would be the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it a wire or cable, something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: LUCIJANA PEKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, like a very, very thin wire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Peko, thank you very much for your coming to assist us, more than once, from what we've been told. I'm sorry about that. And thank you very much for the assistance you've given us. You are now free to go and go back to your home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One procedural matter, if I may. I'll be as short as possible. I'm mindful of Your Honour's direction concerning submissions as to authenticity of documents. Now, in this regard, I'd like to mention, and I don't think Mr. Petrovic will disagree, that prior to Ms. Peko's testifying in this matter, we had agreed between us that P35 as it was then known - now, as it is, the preliminary report, if I may, as it is now known - would be submitted by way of agreement. And on the day of the hearing itself, Mr. Petrovic, as I understand, requested to change his agreement to the fact that he was only agreeing to the parts -- to submit the parts that Ms. Peko had worked on. That's Mr. Petrovic's right, of course. But I would like to state that this was mentioned to us at the very last minute. And I would like to know if Mr. Petrovic is intending to challenge the admissibility of this document even when Dr. Kaiser comes. Because if that is the case, it has been done at the very last minute and we would perhaps have to seek an additional witness in order to tender this document. I would hope it would not come to that. I don't think it should come to that because Dr. Kaiser can speak to the whole document. But I'd like to know where Mr. Petrovic is going with this matter. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, can you assist?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to ask your indulgence, and might I be allowed to answer the question on Monday morning when we reconvene in this courtroom? Because he's not the next witness, the one that we're discussing at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will that be convenient, Mr. Kaufman, or is there some time urgency?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: There is a matter of time urgency, Your Honour, because Dr. Kaiser is due to arrive on Saturday and he'll be proofed in advance of his evidence next week. So we would like to know where we stand in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps you might give some consideration to the matter over the next break, Mr. Petrovic, and we'll raise it again following the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, while you're on your feet, Mr. Petrovic: The question of the photograph which was tendered earlier but in a very, very poor quality form, and which has now been provided in a better quality form, can you indicate how you see the position in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your indulgence, may my colleague Mr. Rodic address the Court on the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Indeed. I was probably in error in not turning to Mr. Rodic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The new photograph, the one we've just been provided, as far as I can see, is just a slightly lighter version of the previous photograph. However, as the Defence has already stressed, it is very important to us to obtain a colour photograph, especially in order to be able to identify the locality where this was taken. So apart from the people that can be seen in the photograph, we can't identify the other necessary elements, the colour and background, in order to be able to determine where the photograph was actually taken. So I would like to ask that, if at all possible, we receive the photograph itself that Mr. Doyle said he had in his possession. As for the second document, related to an illegible copy of the military districts, showing the military districts, on the document that I have just received, this is clearer. You can see Sarajevo and Trebinje better, and we can see that they are military districts. I can just discern that up where it says "Sarajevo," it says the 2nd. I'm not sure whether it is the 4th Military District on this other document, but you can assess that for yourselves. So I will accept your decision on the matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you sit, Mr. Rodic, I agree this is not in colour, but it seems that this is a very much different quality of print from the one which was before us when the witness was here, and I must say that it seems to me that it quite clearly depicts the general locality in which this photograph was taken. It seems very clear that there is a glass structure, a panel, with a door, an unusual architectural shaping behind the three people that can be seen in some detail, and that is repeated further back in the room, as one can see looking at the photograph, with a brick wall to the right. And I'm a little unclear why you say that you cannot identify from this sufficiently the location where the photograph was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree with the description you've just given us. However, at the same time, we can notice that behind Mr. Doyle is a fairly important portion of the photograph, which is dark. That's one point. And the second point: Whether the brick is yellow in colour, red, or some other colour, we do not know from this photograph, because different types of bricks are, of course, used in construction work. So it would be important for identification purposes and also because of the other elements, and also the rank of the accused, to which Mr. Doyle pointed. It is difficult to discern anything about that here, whereas we can see that on the chest, on the left side of the chest, there is something there. So I'm sure that a colour photograph would help us to clarify that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The colour may or may not -- colour is one issue; clarity is another. I'd have thought from this black-and-white presentation, it is clear that the bricks are light in colour, because the mortar is contrasting and dark. I agree, we cannot know the precise colour of the bricks, but at least it would appear they are light bricks. And the point is that you are unlikely to be able to identify a building just from the colour of a brick wall. It is necessary to see a brick wall in conjunction with the other features that appear in the photograph. And the glass partition and door appears to be a quite distinctive item, especially as it is repeated further down in the room, and I'd have thought that was a very significant architectural feature that ought to have assisted considerably in your identification of the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's just been pointed out, of course, that light is clearly coming in from the left-hand side of the photograph, because it slants across the photograph. The assistant to Colonel Doyle, who is on the left, the light comes across his face, but it comes across the chest and the waist of your client in the middle, if you can see the slanting light. So that would assist with the location of the windows. Now, a colour photograph is not going to show us any more of the building. It would simply add colour to what is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the final decision is yours, of course, but I think that because of what I said earlier on -- yes, I'm clear on what you say about the window. That is clearly visible. But the portion behind Mr. Doyle is dark, so that I have no identification there. It is the position of the Defence that a colour photograph would be much more helpful to us, but of course the final decision rests with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In view of the time, rather than commencing a new witness now, we think it would be more practical to have the break a little early, and during that break we can give consideration to this question of the photograph. We will break now for the usual morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would mention the matter of the photograph which came into evidence through the witness Colonel Doyle and which had been the subject of submissions in which the Chamber took the view that the Defence's concern at the quality of that which was before us during the evidence were well-founded and that there was justification for attempts to be made to obtain the original or a better quality, bearing in mind that the need for the original had not been apparent to the Defence earlier, and had arisen, it seems, only during the course of the evidence of Colonel Doyle, and the colonel's understanding that the original was, he thought, although not entirely confidently, was stored in his attic in Ireland, a home which he had left to move to New York, so that it would be of considerable inconvenience for him to have to try and find it. The Chamber has been provided with a far better quality reproduction of that photograph by the Office of the Prosecutor and has heard the submissions of Mr. Rodic concerning this. The Chamber is of the view that the quality of that which is now provided is most significantly better than the version we had during the evidence of Colonel Doyle, and it is our view that this quality is sufficient to meet the concerns which had persuaded the Chamber earlier that further efforts should be made by the Office of the Prosecutor to obtain either the original or a better Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. quality. For that reason, we would regard what has now been provided as an adequate discharge of the request we made to the Office of the Prosecutor about the photograph and would not require further efforts to be made. We are conscious of what Mr. Rodic has said, but in the course of his submissions, views were put to him by me which express generally the view of the Chamber that the photograph copy now available to the Defence should be reasonably adequate for the purpose that has been indicated to us by Mr. Rodic. That having been said, clearly I can take it that the Office of the Prosecutor would be aware that if by chance it happened that Colonel Doyle were in Ireland, he would be encouraged to seek to provide the original, but we see that the interests of justice do not require that we make any formal order or request to that effect. Now, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution's next witness to be examined by Mr. Re is Mr. Mato Valjalo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If the witness could be called.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just inquire: There was another matter pending that was to be deliberated upon by Defence during the break. Mr. Kaufman is remaining for that. Shall we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I overlooked that. Mr. Petrovic, the question of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll try as concisely as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you mind just waiting one moment? I'm having -- just be seated, please, while counsel puts a submission. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to try to elaborate on the problem and to bring up several aspects of it. The first point, something I'm sure you're well aware of, the indictment against my client is composed of precisely defined 500 structures, approximately, which were allegedly damaged or destroyed on the 6th of December, 1991. About 500 structures were specifically mentioned. The time of damage was recorded, the degree of damage, the exact addresses, and the purposes those structures or buildings served. And, Your Honour, as you know full well, that is in attachment 2 that goes with the indictment. Now, how many damaged structures in this attachment, the same number of reports exists on damages, and these have been collected in the preliminary report that we have been discussing over the past few days. And as we were able to hear from the previous witness, each report is separate, each one was compiled by one of the individuals charged by the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments, it was looked through and signed individually by the person who wrote the report. The preliminary report itself is none other than a collection of individual notes or minutes about the damage sustained. So it is not something that is a synthetic product. It is not something that somebody looked at together and drew conclusions on that basis. It is just a collection of individual, autonomous reports, and each of the reports states the name of the person who compiled them. Theoretically speaking, Your Honour, the Defence team of Mr. Strugar, in view of the fact that we're dealing with individually stated structures which have been individually listed in the indictment, the Defence of General Strugar, and I hope you share my opinion, theoretically speaking, of course, would have the right, reason, and grounds for examining each of those 500 structures and challenging them. I emphasise the word "theoretical" because of course we are mindful of time, and that is the concern of the Trial Chamber and our concern as well, as well as all the other participants in these proceedings. So what is all this about, Your Honour? As I said, it is a collection of reports. Mr. Kaiser is one of the individuals who, in the same way, just like the lady who was here to testify a moment ago, compiled individual notes on the damages sustained. Now, what is important in this regard must be said. Mr. Kaiser is not the author. Mr. Kaiser is a counsellor, an advisor. He's not somebody who represents the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments. And you can see for yourselves in the introduction of the report itself, in B/C/S, the page is 01069061, or rather, in the English-language version, the number is as follows: Page L0061414. So that, then, is the introduction to this collection of individual reports and notes on the damages sustained. You can see who stands behind the preliminary report there. So it is the director of the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Monuments. That is the man who signed it and wrote the introduction which was presented to the Trial Chamber for review. In addition to this, on page 0106969058, you can see who the authors are of that preliminary report, although let me emphasise once again that this is something that is not a synthetic product; it is a collection of individual activities on the part of individual people. So the last page I mentioned in the English translation is 0061412. Therefore, Mr. Kaiser neither represents an institution, nor is he one of the authors. Mr. Kaiser himself, and that is what the Defence can accept, can come here to testify about something he himself did. So he can testify about those notes and minutes and reports that he himself signed. Mrs. Peko told her [as interpreted], and I asked her precisely, because of what is happening here now, she said quite simply that what she wrote, what she saw, was not controlled by anybody, it was not redacted by anybody or edited; it is quite simply something that she herself wrote, and in that form submitted for the preliminary report without influence from anyone, from any side. Now, for all these reasons, I don't think that Mr. Kaiser can be an individual who will take it upon himself to testify about the entire report, whereas he actually -- what he actually saw and testifies about is only a segment of that report. You have dozens of pages signed by Mr. Kaiser within that report, but also, Your Honours, you have several hundred pages where no mention is made of Mr. Kaiser at all. And so in the interests of justice, in our opinion, the evidence that is introduced through Mr. Kaiser must be restricted and limited to his actual part and his reporter notes on the investigations he conducted and verified by placing his signature to those pages. I apologise for taking so much of the Court's time, but I do believe that this will help you in your deliberations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Kaufman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, having heard my learned friend's submissions, I cannot help but notice that there seems to be a certain amount of internal, illogical argument. Whilst Mr. Petrovic says that he wishes to save time and avoid calling each and every author of each and every site in the report, which would take a lot of time -- it can be done, but it would take an immense amount of time, he also says, on the other hand, that Dr. Kaiser can only testify to the actual parts of the report that he signed and witnessed. Now, Dr. Kaiser is registered in the list of people appended to the beginning of this document as a consultant. There are four authors, and those authors may be brought, if necessary. I would submit it is not necessary to bring these authors, and I would submit furthermore that it is sufficient to allow Dr. Kaiser to deal with the document as a whole and allow the document to be it admitted as an exhibit through Dr. Kaiser as a whole. According to the precedent of this Tribunal, there is no need for Dr. Kaiser to be an author, I would submit, and furthermore, that familiarity with the contents of the document - and in this matter I mean Dr. Kaiser's intimate familiarity with the documents - is sufficient. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dr. Kaiser oversaw the conduct of the whole of this operation. As Your Honours heard from the last witness, Ms. Peko, they were working to a time schedule. Dr. Kaiser was there from the outset, from when the methodology was instituted. He was the person who instituted the methodology, along with Dr. Bruno Carnez, who will not be testifying, and he oversaw the conduct of this operation from its inception to its conclusion. And to that extent, I would submit that he is familiar with the contents of the report and it should be permissible to allow that document to be submitted as an exhibit through Dr. Kaiser. Otherwise, we will indeed need to call a large number of witnesses in order to submit each and every report in separate, in a separate manner. I would like to furthermore mention that my learned friend has mentioned that the indictment includes in its annex a list of approximately 500 buildings, for which there are 500 reports, but the Defence, as far as I understood it, and from a perusal of the Defence pre-trial brief, although it is not evidence, but a perusal of the Defence pre-trial brief does not deny that considerable damage was caused to the Old Town on the 6th of December. So I would submit that the legal requirements of proving the damage should not be too difficult to fulfil in this case, proving damage, and not just damage but extensive damage, for the purposes of the counts alleged in the indictment. However, having said that, I will return to my initial submission and beg that Dr. Kaiser be allowed to admit this report in its entirety and that it be admitted as an exhibit through him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, very briefly in relation to what my learned friend said. The Defence totally challenges the annex to the indictment, and that is quite clear from our pre-trial motion. So lest there be any misunderstanding or lack of clarity on that part, it is important to mention that. General Strugar is being indicted for each and every individual building, and individual reports, separate reports, were filed for each and every building. I believe that you will agree with me that, theoretically speaking, in relation to each and every building, General Strugar is entitled to put questions with regard to every one of these individual buildings. And this feeling is only heightened after having heard the previous witness. In our opinion, we therefore have the right to express this concern, which is great in terms of the accuracy of what these reports contain. I'm not going to infer anything now on the basis of what the previous witness said, but I will just say that there is heightened concern on our part in terms of the methodology in which all of this was done. Your Honours, all of this should be held against our client then, and we simply cannot allow Mr. Strugar to be accountable for all of that, for each and every individual building and all that damage sustained. Perhaps my learned friends will smile or laugh at what I say now, but, Your Honours, this entire problem could be redressed easily if, quite simply, if we were to talk about those buildings that were destroyed, without going into 500 different buildings. Let them eliminate annex 2 to the indictment and then it will be much easier to discuss it. I'm sure they are going to only laugh about this. But if they do away with that, we are going to save an enormous amount of time. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, what has changed about this? The question of damage was well known to you for some time, and as I understand it from Mr. Kaufman, you were prepared earlier to agree to the tendering of the whole document. Is there some new development in the case which has caused you to change your approach?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, in relation to what you've said just now, I take upon myself this responsibility. I talked to Mr. Kaufman without having discussed it beforehand with other members of the team. So what is this all about? It seemed to me at one point in time that it was more practical, because of the photographs that I presented to you on several occasions, that this should perhaps be marked for identification purposes or in some other way, so that it would be accessible to you, so when I refer to a particular photograph, I can make easy reference to it. Because I copied all of this. You did not accept it. You did not admit it into evidence. It created confusion, what I was doing with the witnesses. So, quite simply, often you did not have the opportunity of seeing this properly, the way you see exhibits. When we looked at the report in detail, both my colleague and I, when we analysed everything that the report contains, when we received a report from our advisor - and I talked to Mr. Kaufman only 10 or 15 days ago, and in the meantime we talked to our advisor too - and then we came to the conclusion that this was quite unacceptable. So this confusion that I caused when talking to Mr. Kaufman some 10 days ago is something that I fully take upon myself, but today we are in a position to take the stand we are taking now. The witness you heard over the past three days has precisely corroborated our position with regard to this particular matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are two aspects to the question of the report presently marked for identification as 51. One is its technical admissibility. The second is the weight which the Chamber in due course might attach to the report as a whole or to individual elements of it. With respect to admissibility, which is the issue presently before the Chamber, if it proves to be the case, as Mr. Kaufman has anticipated, that the proposed witness Mr. Kaiser will be able to indicate that he had oversight of the preparation of the whole of the report, the Chamber would be prepared to admit the report on that basis. Just what weight would then be attached to individual components of it will be a matter for the future consideration of the Chamber, in light of the whole of the evidence as to damage. It is clear in this matter that the position of the Defence is developing, changing, as the trial proceeds. We would -- in view of some comments made by Mr. Petrovic, we would encourage discussions between Defence and Prosecuting counsel over this question of damage. It appears to the Chamber that it may well be that common ground can be reached. There may be areas where there can be mutual agreement, certainty about damage, and if that can be done, it might avoid a great deal of time and work, both for Defence and Prosecution, and enable that aspect of the case to be put to one side so that some of the bigger issues that are more critical can be concentrated on. So we would encourage further consideration to those matters and discussion between counsel for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just address that issue? In fairness to both parties. Earlier last week, I did address with Mr. Petrovic perhaps the wisdom of trying to arrive at some stipulations based on a review of the pre-trial brief, and he had indicated willingness to sit down and do so. So the dialogue is open and perhaps it may be able to materialise. We can't guarantee that anything will come out of it, but the dialogue is certainly open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, anything the Chamber can do to encourage that, please understand, we support and encourage it fully. Now, sir, I thank you for waiting patiently while we dealt with that matter. If you would please stand and take the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated now. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please give the Trial Chamber your full name.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Mato Valjalo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth, Mr. Valjalo?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The 18th of May, 1948.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you live in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I was born in Konavle, and I live in the Old Town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you live in the Old Town of Dubrovnik in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the address in the Old Town of Dubrovnik where you lived in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Prijeko, number 19.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do JNA military service; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. I did my service in Dubrovnik while the army was there. It was between 1967 and 1969. In 1970, the army left Dubrovnik. Excuse me. The army left Dubrovnik and went to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your occupation today, Mr. Valjalo?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I'm a driver in the Dubrovacko Neretvanska district, and I drive the head of district, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the municipal authority or the local council, and is the person you drive for the mayor?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. It's different now. Before there was this different system that involved municipalities, whereas now there are towns and districts. So I work for the district and the head of the district. So it encompasses a broader region, from Prevlaka to Ploce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long have you been driving for local officials connected with the municipality or the larger area?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: In 1981 I came to the Municipal Assembly, and I've been there ever since.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, would you be able to speak a little bit more loudly so that the interpreters can hear you and translate your words into English for the non-Croatian speakers in the Court.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the military in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a civilian?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, I was, a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: And I had the same job that I have today. But at that time, this big district did not exist. At that time, I drove the president of the Executive Council of the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Mr. Zeljko Sikic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your duties in driving Mr. Sikic? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, before the war broke out, of course, we did what was done. I drove these officials in different areas, in towns, two different towns, whatever was necessary. There were also other high officials who came to Dubrovnik, and I was even involved in the protocol that dealt with foreign visitors too, and I was actually driving them as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that that was in the Old Town and the town of -- the larger town of Dubrovnik and the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, the Old Town and the entire town of Dubrovnik, and also the airport at Cilipi. I would drive someone to the airport or meet them there. And also, different meetings were held in other municipalities, and when it was necessary to drive people there, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you mobilised during the war, that is, in 1991, 1992, 1993, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: My work obligation was again that of a driver attached to the Executive Council, without any weapons, without a rifle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about a uniform? Did you wear civilian clothes or a uniform in your duties driving Mr. Sikic around?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Civilian. Civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made a statement to the -- an Office of the Prosecutor investigator on the 20th of May, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I'm correcting something for the record which I have advised my learned friends of before, which we found out in proofing when we were conferring yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement, you described Mr. Sikic as the president of the Territorial Defence. Was that a correct description of his duties in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. The Territorial Defence was something different. That's not what Mr. Sikic was. He was president of the Executive Council. And at that time, he was also president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you -- are you aware of where the headquarters of the Territorial Defence were located in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, the National Defence? Well, you see, I think that was near the medical centre in Lapad. That's where the military department was during the former Yugoslavia, and then the Territorial Defence was down there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any Territorial Defence facilities being located in the Old Town of Dubrovnik in September, October, November, or December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present in Dubrovnik during shelling in September, October, November, or December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I was, until I was wounded on the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to tell the Trial Chamber where the Serb positions were during the shelling in that period?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: They were above the town, in Zarkovica, Bosanka, on the other side. I don't know. On the Imperijal Fortress, on Mount Srdj, that is where our army was. Underneath that hill there was a bunker, a bunker where the enemy army was. The town itself was free below the highway, and all the way up to Sustjepan. Sustjepan was the defence front line when they had already taken Mokosica, the western part, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, can I just ask you to keep your voice up again and just go back a moment. A moment ago I referred to Serb positions. What I actually meant to say was JNA positions, and I apologise for that. In your answer, were you referring to JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: JNA positions that I could see from town were on the hill of Zarkovica, where a cannon could be seen that was shooting at the Old Town. There were bunkers underneath Mount Srdj, the Imperijal Fortress, about 100 to 200 metres away there were soldiers. There was ammunition also on the hill of Zarkovica, then also they were on Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the JNA positions. What about the Croat positions? Where were they?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The Croat positions were on the fortress of Srdj, the Imperijal Fortress, as it is called, on Srdj. And perhaps below the highway. I don't know. And on the other side, I can only say that they were in Sustjepan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Valjalo. I want to ask you about the 6th of December, 1991. Where were you on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
