utterances.text: On the 6th of December I was at the Municipal Assembly. In the early morning hours -- I don't know the exact time when the attack began, but it did start from the eastern side, coming from the eastern side, not the west, I'm sorry. And we --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll just take you back. Where did you spend the night of the 5th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I spent the night at the Municipal Assembly of Dubrovnik. I was on duty there, by the telephone, and the attack had already started against Konavle. Konavle was already attacked by Montenegro and I was in the Municipal Assembly that morning too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said an attack occurred. How did you come to know that an attack occurred?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Detonations were heard. My relatives from Konavle had already moved to Dubrovnik. They were staying at my apartment. So I called them immediately and I said that I hoped it wouldn't be that way. And I went up to the top of the building of the Municipal Assembly to see where the shells were coming from and where they were falling. I saw that they were targeting the highway and also below the highway, the old road leading to the highway. I'm sorry. Can you repeat what you said just now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to ask you about is the 6th of December, 1991. Now, I'll just stop there. You said something about your relatives. You had a wife and children in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. I had a wife and children. Unfortunately, they were supposed to go because we were left without electricity, water, a telephone. There were relatives there, small children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, were your wife and children living with you in the Old Town of Dubrovnik; and if so, until when?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: They were living there, but as Dubrovnik was constantly being shelled, you couldn't stay there with the small children any more. There was no electricity, we had nothing to eat, and so they had to leave town. And they went by ship. I don't remember the exact date. And all my relatives left as well, and they ended up at Rabac. My wife and my children were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Not too many details on this. What I want you to tell the Trial Chamber is, to the best of your recollection, when did they leave for Rabac, leaving you in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The month was October, but I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you remained behind in the Old Town. Did you remain behind in your house or flat?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I remained behind in the Old Town, and my house was also damaged. The windows were shattered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, what I want you to do is listen very carefully to the question I'm asking you, and just please for the moment concentrate on that one and I'll move to the other part in a moment. Now, what I want you to tell me is: You stayed behind. Who, if anyone, did you stay behind with after your family went to Rabac?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The person who stayed behind with me, he is deceased now, was my father-in-law, my wife's father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he stayed behind with you, and did you continue working for Mr. Sikic, driving him, after your family left for Rabac?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. I continued working. I drove Mr. Sikic least, actually, because if anybody came to town, foreigners and others, like Mr. Kuchner, for example, I would drive them. I've forgotten all the other names but when any dignitary came to town, I would drive them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you staying with your father-in-law in December; that's the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th of December, 1991, in your apartment in the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. When there was no shooting. But when shells were falling, then we took to the shelter, and the shelter was a school in the centre of town, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about a specific attack on the 6th of December, 1991. Where was your father-in-law in the early hours of the 6th of December, 1991? That's before about 5.00, 6.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: On that day, we were in my apartment. We spent the night there, and in the morning when we got up, I shaved, we heard the shells falling, and from my own house you can see Mount Srdj and I saw shells falling at the Imperijal Fortress on Mount Srdj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll just stop you. About what time was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: That was approximately -- well, I think it began at 6.00 a.m., perhaps a little before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do? I'm sorry. I withdraw that. What did your father-in-law do when the shelling began?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: After the shelling, the alarm sounded for general danger, and my father-in-law went to the shelter, and the shelter was in the Institute for the Reconstruction of Dubrovnik. I myself stayed behind a few minutes after him, because I think I was shaving or doing something like that, and then I went to work as I did every day. I went outside, onto Stradun. I heard some terrible shooting around town, and I wasn't conscious of what was going on, but I rushed -- I started running. And after I had taken several steps, a shell fell right behind me. It landed some 50 or 40 metres behind me. I was seriously wounded as a result, from the impact of the blow. I felt terrible -- a terrible headache. I thought my head had been shattered. I felt some shrapnel hitting me in my legs, and I had a piece of shrapnel in my head, and I lost consciousness as a result. But I was aware -- I came to when I started getting up from the pavement of Stradun, and I realised that it was a shell. I felt something warm over my leg, and I put my hand down to feel that point, and my hand was all bloody. I felt a warm sensation behind my neck, and I put my hand to that place, and it was all bloody too. But luckily, I was able to get to my feet and run away and reach the town cafe, the central cafe in town. And I told them there that I had been wounded. They bandaged my wounds, my leg, stopped the bleeding, as far as they were able to, and they had a spray which they sprayed my neck with to stop the bleeding. And from the Municipal Assembly, they learnt straight away that I had been wounded, they called the ambulance, the emergency service. But as the shells were still falling, the ambulance wasn't able to reach me. When I entered the central coffee bar, the shells began falling onto the Old Town one after another. And the church of St. Blaise was damaged too, and the shrapnels were flying into the central cafe. Many of the buildings in town were damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I stop you there? You went to the cafe and you were wounded, and there was no ambulance. Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, the ambulance wasn't able to arrive, so I stood there for about an hour. My friends kept me from losing consciousness. They gave me some lemon juice. And then two gentlemen wearing camouflage uniform, they were going round town and collecting up the dead and wounded. When I myself was wounded, a man behind me was killed, the late Mr. Urban, and this happened in the Old Town. He was killed while filming the war going on. These two men picked me up and they took me to hospital, despite all the shells that were falling, and the hospital is at Medarevo, that is to say, on the opposite side of town, of Lapad. I was admitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to stop you there for a moment. You mentioned Pavo Urban, Mr. Urban, and you said he was killed while filming in a similar vicinity to you. Did you actually see, witness his death?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I wasn't an eyewitness of his death, because when the first shell fell - I think it was on Stradun - I was wounded by that first shell falling. And I managed to reach the central cafe. And when those two men arrived, the waiter from the cafe went outside, and he heard a car arriving. He thought it was the ambulance. It wasn't the ambulance, it was these two men with a van who went around collecting -- what they were doing. And he said: Sir, leave him alone. He's dead. I didn't know who they meant at that point. But they said: There's a man who's seriously wounded here, so try and save his life, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago, before I stopped you, you were telling the Trial Chamber about going to the hospital. What treatment did you receive at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: They x-rayed me at the hospital and said they had managed to extract some of the shrapnel, although I had a lot of fragments. The one that lodged in my head, actually, the neurosurgeon wasn't in Dubrovnik at the time so they weren't able to extract that piece of shrapnel. Many wounded people came into the hospital that day, 15 or 16. There were 19 dead on the 6th of December, so they were kept busy --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So can you please tell the Trial Chamber what injuries you received and what was treated at the hospital. You've mentioned shrapnel in your leg and the back of your head. Can you please summarise for the Trial Chamber where you were hit and what the doctors did.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I was hit -- can I get up to show you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honours have no objection?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I was hit in my right leg. I had two pieces of shrapnel here, and you can see the scars, if you want to look. There's one on this side here, two in my back, one pierced my chest and another lodged in -- another damaged my muscle here, head muscle. It was three centimetres and they extracted that at the hospital in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just so we get it on the transcript, can you please remain standing for a moment, Mr. Valjalo.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just so the transcript is accurate. You were indicating with your hand your right knee area and the back of your thigh on the right side, and also the back -- you put your hand on the back of the right side of your back, and also touched the back of your head and your front right-hand side. Were those the places you just touched? Because when you said "here," we don't pick that up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the spots. And I have the diagnosis and findings from the hospital, and it says exactly where those spots were. The muscle in my thigh, the lower leg, another one in my thigh, one or two in my back, right shoulder, and one of them pierced my chest, and there was another to the back of my head, the top of my spine. And I have the release form or discharge papers from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you operated on at the hospital in Dubrovnik? You can sit down.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you operated on at the hospital in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. I was on the table while they were x-raying me. They didn't operate. They did take out, extract certain fragments from my leg. Others remained lodged there. And they said that they couldn't extract the other one because they were afraid of damaging me. And then I was sent on for further treatment to the hospital in Rijeka, with the second convoy that arrived in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was that you were transferred to Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I think it was the 14th of February, the second convoy. President Mesic and the rest were in the first convoy. The second convoy that arrived, when it went back, I think that was sometime -- actually, it was a Friday. I think the date was the 14th. I'm not quite sure. I'm not sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a moment. You've described the injuries you received. Did they affect your life after you were hit by the shrapnel? Are there any things that you could do before that you can't do now?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Of course there are. When I came back from the treatment at the Rijeka hospital, I carried on working straight away, because we had more work, as the county was being set up. The shrapnel caused me quite a lot of problems and I felt poorly for quite some time. So I went to Zagreb for a check-up. They examined me there. And in Zagreb, they found another piece of shrapnel lodged in my lungs, which I knew nothing about. And I still feel pain in my leg. There is a certain amount of swelling. I suffer headaches frequently. Until I was wounded, I never took five aspirins for a headache before in my life. Now I have to take medication twice a week. And I mostly react to changes in the weather, when my neck hurts, because I think that my circulation in that part of my neck is poor, and that's where one of the nerves was damaged as a result of the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you still feel pain in your leg. Have the injuries affected your mobility in any way? That is, are there things you could do before that you can't do -- you couldn't do afterwards or can't do now?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, there are. I used to run before. I can't run any more, at least just for brief periods when I feel pain. And it's risky business having the fragments of shrapnel extracted now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how long you were unconscious for in Stradun after the shell struck or exploded behind you?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: After the shell exploded, I felt this impact on my legs. Actually, I felt something warm. And when I fell, I probably knocked my head on the paving, because my nose was bruised. But I regained consciousness fairly quickly. Had I stayed down for another minute or two, I probably wouldn't have been able to get up, because there was shelling all the time. One shell after another, all over town. I don't know whether there was a single spot where the shells didn't fall. The palace where the summer games were held and Boskovic's house was shelled, and I wasn't able to see anything after that. I just listened to the radio broadcasts while I was in hospital. They said what was on fire. They asked Italy's assistance. They asked for helicopters to be sent in to put out the fires.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A moment ago you just mentioned the palace where the summer games were held. Did you mean by that the Festival Palace?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. They were their offices on Stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want you to describe or tell the Trial Chamber what your feelings were or how you felt as you were walking down Stradun and hearing shelling on the 6th of December, 1991. What was going on in your mind?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, yes. Well, I don't know. But I never thought the Old Town would come under attack. I know that there was shooting up there, but unfortunately, I didn't think right because I fared badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you scared when you were walking down Stradun on the morning of the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, yes, I was. As soon as I saw so much shelling up at Srdj, Mount Srdj, I thought one of them fell closer to town, but I couldn't actually see. But that was the first time that I was running out of fear; I was running because I was afraid. And while I was running -- actually, I didn't manage to take two or three steps when the shell hit me. I thought that it had blown my head off. And I know where the hole is to this day, although there are no remnants of it, but I know exactly where it was. I thought my eardrums had exploded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised, Mr. Valjalo, that there was shelling on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I was surprised from the very first day. I was surprised, because we didn't deserve that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described the injuries you -- I'm sorry, you wish to continue your answer?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Later on, later on I saw that nothing should take me by surprise, because the shells fell over everything and everyone. Children, grandmothers, schools, hospitals, none of them were saved. I saw the Belvedere Hotel in flames, I saw the old Imperijal Hotel up in flames, so I wasn't surprised by anything, because nobody was spared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "later on," were you referring to the 6th of December or another time?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, even before the 6th of December, and after that, when I returned from Rijeka, from my treatment and rehabilitation there, that was February, I think the 26th of February, I started working again in March, right up to May there were still shells falling and shooting coming from all sides, from planes, aircraft. They shelled the fortress straight away, the fortress at Mount Srdj. That was on the 6th of December. No. Not the 6th of December. On the 1st of October. I apologise. On the 1st of October when that all started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to your treatment at the Dubrovnik hospital in Rijeka. Did you also receive treatment at the thalassotherapy in Opatija?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Luckily, I was treated by an excellent neurosurgeon at the hospital in Rijeka, and I was given injections two or three times a day to clear the wound. And they then sent me for thalassotherapy rehabilitation because I wasn't able to walk. While my wounds were still hot I was able to run, but once everything cooled down I wasn't able to rise from my bed. The whole of my right side went rigid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you at that hospital from the 9th of January, 1992, until the 26th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What time are Your Honours intending taking the break? I just noticed it's midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not for a quarter of an hour or longer, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If it please Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, you've described injuries to yourself. What about your house? Was your house damaged in the shelling attack on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: On the 6th of December, 1991, my house was damaged, and so was my neighbour's house. Because, actually, it's a semi-detached house, a half-half, so our houses were damaged, and my car that was parked outside the town walls, in a place called Buza, I had a Volkswagen, and that was destroyed too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Just concentrate on your house at the moment. Can you describe the damage to your house from the shelling on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot, because I wasn't able to go back to my house and see it. My friends just covered it up to prevent the rain from coming in, covered the windows up. But the damage isn't that bad. The damage wasn't that bad. My neighbour's house was damaged more badly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did your friends cover up to prevent the rain coming in? Was that the roof?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: They covered the roof. They covered it with some kind of plastic sheets or something thin. But of course that wouldn't last long, so then again something had to be done about the roof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that your roof was damaged on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Because my father-in-law came to my house every day. I even had a parakeet that they fed every day throughout the war, and it's alive still. So every day, even under the shells, we took food to the parakeet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying your father-in-law told you the house or the roof of the house was damaged from shelling on the 6th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's what my father-in-law said to me. There were other damages too. Should I mention all of it? Two or three times I had to change all the window panes. Also the water installations were destroyed. Shells fell on the other street above Stradun, called Prijeko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: It was also on the 6th of December. Some shells fell on other days too, but it's hard for a person to remember all of that now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When -- doing your best, to your best recollection, when did you have to replace the glass in your windows as a result of shelling in the area?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I think it was after the month of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: 1992. Because my wife and children weren't at the apartment yet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that your Volkswagen was destroyed that was parked outside the Old Town, I think you said in Buza. When was it destroyed and how was it destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Again, my friends told me about this. The car was in the street, and they said to me: Your car was totally damaged. It was hit by lots of shrapnel. And other cars were damaged too. Some of them had even burned down. This was in the northern part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us -- you've told the Trial Chamber that you lived in the Old Town in September, October -- sorry, lived and worked in the Old Town of Dubrovnik in September, October, November, and the first six days of December 1991. In that period, did you see any Croatian artillery or armaments in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, not then or not before that, not in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about armed Croatian soldiers? Did you ever see any armed Croatian soldiers in the Old Town in that period?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Armed? No. Perhaps two or three times I saw soldiers in camouflage uniform who had a pistol on their belts or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: These were probably the ones who were at the positions elsewhere, and then they would come home to change or to bathe, using sea water, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever any outgoing fire from the Old Town towards JNA positions when you were living and working there in September, October, November, and the first few days of December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Croatian military institutions located in the Old Town when you were living and working there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, no. I did not see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to clarify something earlier. I may have missed it. When I asked you about Mr. Sikic's position, did you say it was the president of the Executive Council of the Crisis Staff or the president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: He was president of the Executive Council. That was the actual office he held. But before the army was formed, there was a Crisis Staff, and this position of president of Crisis Staff was held by the president of the Executive Council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to conclude your evidence in chief, Mr. Valjalo, I wish to show you some photographs, two photographs and a map, and ask you to mark on them. I also wish to show you three medical -- three of your medical records.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I intend to show the witness copies of Exhibits P18, P12, and P17. That's a photograph of Stradun, a photograph of -- overhead photograph of the Old Town, and a map of the Old Town of Dubrovnik. First I'm showing the -- I'm first showing the witness a copy of P17. I'm sorry. Lest there be any confusion, if that is the original, I intend to show the witness a Prosecution copy which we'll have the witness mark. It's an identical copy of the same photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we first take a look at this map? Can we just see the original, briefly, the one given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No, not that one. The one that you are putting there now. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, if you can just turn to your left, you'll see a photograph on an overhead projector we call the ELMO. Can you please take the blue marker pen, and I want you to circle, firstly, your -- firstly, can you find and see your house in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I can't do it very precisely, but it's here, within these two streets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'll get you to do firstly is just point to it on the screen and then maybe you can put it in front of you and write on it. It might be easier. First can you point out -- just point to where your house is. Don't do it on that screen; no one can see you.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Can you see it here now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. We can see that now. Just I wish you -- I want you to point out where the Municipal Assembly is.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thirdly, I wish you to point out where the spot where you were hit by the shrapnel is in Stradun.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the fourth thing I wish you to point out is where your car was when it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to take the pen and draw a circle, and in the circles, mark 1, 2, 3, and 4. 1 is for your house; 2 is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Take it step by step, I would suggest, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, if you want to take it off and get a better picture of it, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've marked "1" on it?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: 1 is the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. 2, I want you to mark a circle with a "2" in it on the Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: On this side, here, in this area. Well, it's not exactly accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 3, the spot -- the approximate spot where you were hit. Have you marked "3" on, Mr. Valjalo?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 4, can you just mark in with a circle and a "4" inside it the spot where your car was parked.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Can it be seen now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not until you put it onto the overhead projector. We can see that. Now, I just want you to do a legend on the side. In the left-hand side, on the border, can you write 1, 2, 3, 4. 1, house; 2, town hall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I suggest, Mr. Re, that the Court Officer might do that, now that the markings are on the map. It will make it easier for the witness if the officer did it. We're waiting for your indication, Mr. Re. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honour is asking me if I have any objection to the usher, certainly not. I just can't see what's going on because it's not on the overhead projector. But if the usher wishes, please write --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be a lot less confusing for the witness if the Court Officer did it. Thank you. Number 1 -- the usher hasn't heard me. Would you be able to write in the margin of the exhibit "1" in a circle. If you'd take over, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Will do. House. Just on the side, in the white border on the left. Tiny little letters. Number 2, Municipal Assembly. Number 3, place of injury. Number 4, car. THE USHER: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you please give it back to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Valjalo, can you please just write your name and sign it at the bottom and put your date, which is the 6th of February, 2004.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: 6th? What's the date today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 6th February 2004.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The next one I wish to show you is a copy of P12, which is the map we've been using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's being set up, the first one will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could that perhaps remain with the witness while he marks the next one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P53.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again with the same blue pen, I want you to perform the same exercise on that map, a circle with a "1" in it for your house.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 2 for the Municipal Assembly. Have you marked the number "2" on?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. I'm looking at this map. I find it different. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 3 for the spot where you were hit by the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 4 for the spot where your Volkswagen was parked when it was destroyed, a circle with a "4" in it.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And could the usher please do the same thing, write 1, 2, 3, and 4 in the margins. If you could do it identically to the one you've just marked before, please. THE USHER: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, can you please also sign -- put your name and sign and date the bottom of that -- of the map, please.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the marked map was on the ELMO only for a split second. Could we please have it placed on the ELMO again so that we could actually see the markings properly. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May that also be tendered into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P54.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I also wish to show the witness a copy of Prosecution Exhibit P18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at that photo, Mr. Valjalo. What is that a photograph of?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I wouldn't know what is actually on this photo. I was injured. I was wounded there. The late Pavo was here. Maybe it's his photograph too. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just said you were injured: "I was wounded there," and you were pointing to a spot on the photograph. Is that a photograph of the place on Stradun where you were when you were injured by shrapnel from the shell?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is Stradun. Yes. I was hit in the middle of Stradun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see the spot on the map, or the place on the map where you were when you were hit?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Approximately here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you say "here," can you again please take that blue pen and mark a large circle with an "X" in the middle, large so that it is quite -- large enough for everyone to see, and put an "X" in the middle of the circle.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I think that this is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you also, please, sign your name on the bottom and put your date on the bottom of this photograph as well.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Would it be appropriate for the usher to mark on the side "place of injury," so that the exhibit never becomes lost. THE USHER: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: May that go on the ELMO so that it can be seen by Mr. Rodic. You tender that as well, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will be received. Is this a convenient moment for a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I only have the three medical records to tender, but if Your Honours wish to break now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you identify and tender those.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The usher will show you your three medical records. Can you please just identify for the record that I'm showing you three medical records, one from the -- the first one is from the clinical hospital in Rijeka --

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- the second one is from the thalassotherapy --

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and that's dated the 9th --

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Opatija --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the record, release form dated 9th of January, 1992. The second one is a record from the thalassotherapy of Opatija, dated the 26th of February, 1992. Will you just identify that that is the record in your hand.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: That's it. These are those documents exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the third one is a release form from the General Hospital in Zagreb, which appears to be undated but relates to treatment in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If Your Honours wish me to read them on to the record and tender them formally after the break, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They can be received as documents, perhaps as one combined exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I note for the record I've -- we've handed up the English and the B/C/S originals at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That concludes the examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And the exhibit number is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The photograph marked by the witness as Prosecution Exhibit P55; the medical records, P56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. We will have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Rodic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Valjalo. I am the counsel Rodic, and I'm going to ask you some questions with respect to your testimony. Before I start, let me tell you that we're very sorry for the injuries you sustained in 1991, and our sympathies on behalf of the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecution, you said that you live in Dubrovnik, in the Old Town, and that you've lived there since 1970; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, in Dubrovnik, but not since 1970 -- not the same address. I am in the Old Town, Prijeko number 19 is the street, and I've lived there since 1988.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since 1988, you say?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly when I was given the flat, but I did live in several apartments. For a time I didn't have an apartment and had to move around, but I think that would be it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Before that particular address, Prijeko Street, did you also live in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to ask the usher for Exhibit P56, which is the discharge papers, the medical documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at that document, and in paragraph 2, it says Valjalo Mato, from Dubrovnik, Domina 28 is the address on the release form from the Rijeka Clinical Hospital Centre, dated the 9th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Where is that? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 1 of the release form, the Clinical Hospital at Rijeka, the date is Rijeka, January 9th, and the address says Od Domina.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: That's a mistake, and I've just realised that. They filled that in -- actually, the employees of the Rijeka hospital filled that in, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how were they able to record this particular address, Od Domina Street number 28?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I was a tenant there. The flat didn't belong to me. But perhaps it's an old address on my ID card. Perhaps it was my old ID card with this old address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you a tenant at that particular address?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I can't remember. Certainly 1985, or rather, from the 1980s onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher show the witness Exhibit P12, a map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know what this address is. I've just noticed it here, realised what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at that, please. Number 1 on the map is what you marked in Prijeko Street, where you lived; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. That is my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you indicate to the Trial Chamber where Od Domina Street is, which has been registered in the form as being your address.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: This is it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's opposite Prijeko Street, right the other end?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. But as I say, the mistake was made by the person filling in the address on the form, on the release form.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do for the time being. And at the clinical hospital in Rijeka, how were the employees able to write down that address there then?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know where they got it from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody know you at the hospital in Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, nobody knew me, either in the hospital or at the centre for thalassotherapy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could they have -- could you have given that piece of data yourself or from your identification card, I assume, your ID?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, yes. They probably found it on one of my documents. Now, what document it was, I can't say. Maybe it was my old, expired ID card. I didn't change it. Perhaps that's where it was. But I can prove ownership of the apartment I live in and the date I have been living there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, with respect to the medical documents, on that first piece of paper, we see that the 9th of January, 1992, Rijeka, is the date; is that right? So that first document relates to Rijeka, with the date of the 9th of January, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The 9th of January, yes. I hope it's correct. They wrote in the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The title of the document is "Release Form," and it includes the information that, from the 16th of December, 1991 to the 9th of January, 1992, you were undergoing treatment at the neurological clinic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, probably, if that's what they've put there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now turn to page 2, please. This is a document from the special thalassotherapy hospital in Opatija. It is another release form from that institution. And on that document, the date is the 26th of February, 1992. In the upper right-hand corner, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Underneath, it says your name, your surname, it says "Dubrovnik," and then the address, Prijeko Street number 19.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in the first paragraph of the release form, it says that you were treated at that hospital from the 9th of January to the 26th of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I assume it's true and correct. I don't suppose they falsified that. They issued the form, so they filled it in and they must know the dates. I can't remember myself, but it must be right, yes. Because I left the Rijeka clinical hospital and went to -- for rehabilitation treatment there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were there from the 9th of January to the 26th of January [as interpreted] 1992, recuperating; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the address given here is Prijeko Street number 19; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you then explain the fact that during the entire time spent in Rijeka and Opatija, without having returned to Dubrovnik during that period of time, that you have two recorded addresses?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I can't explain that. I don't know where they got the second address from and where it has come from. All I can say is that the Prijeko 19 one is the correct address.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what indicates that the first address is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I was a tenant in that flat, ten years ago, ten years prior to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did somebody know that at the hospital in Rijeka, that you were a tenant, that you were subletting?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the third document is the release form from the third hospital, that is to say, the General Hospital in Zagreb, and in paragraph 1 it says that you were there undergoing treatment from the 3rd of March to the 25th of March, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's go back to the first document, the Rijeka document. Take a look at that now, please. It says there that on the 16th of December, you arrived at the hospital in Rijeka. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, probably. I don't remember the date, but it must be correct if they entered it onto the form. I got to Rijeka on a Saturday, or rather, Sunday morning was when I arrived. I spent the night at Rabac, which is where my wife and children were, and on Monday morning I went to the clinical hospital in Rijeka. Now, what date that was, it must be the date recorded there in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that among the medical documentation there is not a single document which relates to the 6th of December, 1991, which is the day of your alleged wounding; is that right? And there is not a single medical document dated the 6th of December from Dubrovnik, the Dubrovnik Hospital at Medarevo either.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Let me check. I would have to check here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Check where?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: There's something missing here, the one from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does your lawyer have that? Who is your lawyer, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I didn't mean lawyer. I mean the person I gave the papers to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, who did you give the papers to? Can you tell us who you gave the papers to?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just have the three documents we mentioned and the translations into English. So what I'm asking you about is not contained amongst those documents. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I think I had it, and I think I handed it over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you possess a document like that at all?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: If not here, then it's in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why didn't you hand it over, why didn't you hand that document over, because it should have been the first document, judging by its importance. We even have documents dated to 1994 that have been attached to the documents submitted, and yet we have no document dated the 6th of December which would confirm that you were wounded in Dubrovnik and that you were treated first in Dubrovnik. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: That is right, yes, but then they didn't write it down here, those who should have. I have it in Dubrovnik, that's for sure. That's certain. Because I went to Rijeka from Dubrovnik, from the Dubrovnik Hospital, and I went -- travelled with the second convoy, and I think that was the 14th of February -- or the 14th of November, rather.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness mentions 14 and 11. Interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I haven't got the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The documents that you're looking at now, that you have before you, did you hand them over when you came to The Hague to testify or was that earlier? Did that take place earlier?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I didn't hand over anything now. Probably before, when the people who were with me contacted me, the colleagues that contacted me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who it was who contacted you, and when?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I can't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you give anybody a statement of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when and to whom?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Two or three years ago, but I forget the names and I haven't got them written down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The person you talked to, how did he introduce himself?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The investigators introduced themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they investigators from the OTP of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you make a statement to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might that be the statement dated the 20th of May, 2000, and that you conducted your conversation with Dirk Hoojikaas in Dubrovnik? Would that be right, Dirk Hoojikaas?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the interview and giving the statement, did you read through the statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you agree with everything it says in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try and jog your memory. In that statement, you say that on the 12th of December, 1991, or around that date, you were taken to Rijeka by ship. On the 27th of December, you say: I was operated on for injuries to my head.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "I have provided Investigator Hoojikaas with a photocopy of a release letter which explains my injuries. I have also provided him with therapy statement dated the 26th of February, 1992 and a follow-up statement of a control examination because of problems I was encountering in 1994." And it says: "I stayed in the hospital in Rijeka until the 26th of February, 1992." The 26th of February, I think you mean. You made a slip of the tongue and said March. It's the third month?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. "Veljaca" is the second month, February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise. Yes, I meant the 26th of February, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes. I can't remember all the dates exactly, but if it says so in the document, then it's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The medical forms and documents that you have before you correspond to the statement you made in your 2000 statement, and so do the medical findings that you handed over to the investigator. When you compare that to the statement and the findings you have before you, they are identical. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: All of that is correct, but I don't know where this release form from Dubrovnik is, and also I don't know about this address, how it got into this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the medical documents you're holding your hands, and also from the statement from the year 2000, in which it is stated what the medical documents that you gave to the investigator were; also, in your statement it cannot be seen that you had any kind of document in your possession from the medical centre in Dubrovnik, dated the 6th of December, 1991, or that you handed such a document over to the investigator. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, maybe I didn't hand it over. I don't know. I just know that this is correct, that that is 100 per cent sure, this wounding of mine. In Dubrovnik, I was in the hospital, and then to the hospital in Rijeka, and then the thalassotherapy in Opatija, and then I felt quite sick, and that's when I went to Zagreb, to the hospital there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I fully agree with what you said just now. Can we agree that right now in this courtroom there is not a single document related to your alleged wounding on the 6th of December, 1991 in Dubrovnik? Isn't that right? Mr. Valjalo, I'm not challenging the fact that you had been wounded. I'm just stating that there is not a single document - I mean, we don't have it - that it was on the 6th of December that you were wounded in Dubrovnik, that is to say, under the circumstances that you described here before the Court; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Can you just read this here, on page 2? "The patient was wounded by shrapnel in different parts of the body. The first surgical treatment was received in Dubrovnik. Treatment continued in Rijeka. And then further treated by physical therapy. His general state at the time of release was improved. Surgical and psychiatric check-up recommended." That is what it says here, except that I haven't got the release form here from Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is correct that there is mention of Dubrovnik, but the date of your wounding and the place of your wounding are not mentioned specifically at all. It only says Dubrovnik. Dubrovnik is a very broad term, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I can provide it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why didn't you do that in 2000?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, in 2000 I had it, and I still have it at my home. I'm sure I do. I gave it at so many places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any special reason why you would not give the investigator that document? Please just wait for me to finish my question and then answer it, because if there's this kind of overlapping, then the interpreters can't do their work. You and I understand each other, of course. So was there any special reason why this initial document was not handed over to the investigator in 2000, or why did you not give it to the Prosecution now when you came to testify in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: There was no special reason.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So why was this not done? This is elementary proof, the basic proof of your wounding on the 6th of December, as you had mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I would have brought it along with me if I realised that they didn't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I object to my learned friend's question, which of course was answered before I could object, which was, "This is elementary proof, the basic proof of your wounding on the 6th of December as you had mentioned." That proposition is just wrong in fact and in law. Your Honours have heard the witness's testimony. That's the proof of it. I don't object to the -- to my friend obviously challenging the witness, but not in that form. I'm objecting to the form of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The point is made, Mr. Rodic. We have the evidence of the witness that it occurred on the 6th. Your point is that there is no hospital record that confirms that. And we have that noted now, so perhaps you might like to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Valjalo, tell me: Where did you exactly do your military service?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I did my military service in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend your entire military service in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. I cannot remember exactly how much time I spent in Trebinje, because I was supposed to take the military driver's examination. That perhaps took three or four weeks, I don't know, but the rest of my term I spent in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you serve in the military?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: In the navy, infantry -- well, naval infantry. I don't know now. What do you call it? The marines, I think. Later on I was transferred to an automobile unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you transferred to the Trebinje Brigade, and is that where you completed this course, this driver's course; and if so, which category did you get?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I had C category from my civilian life, so I only took the military driver's exam in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: You finished your military service in 1969, so did you go on working as a driver, a professional driver?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me where you started working then as a driver after completing your military service?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: First I was briefly employed in Konavle, in the field of Konavle. That's where I drove a tractor, did the plowing. That was for about half a year. And then in 1970 I transferred to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me: After completing your military service, were you registered as a reservist with some military office?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: In Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which unit? In which reserve unit of the Territorial Defence were you?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I don't know. I was in an auto unit, an automobile unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this unit have a name? Was it more specifically designated? Also, what was the strength of the unit?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I can't say. When they'd call me up for these reserve activities, then it was some kind of an accompanying battalion or whatever it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you called up for military exercises within the reserve before 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, I was, several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this only around Dubrovnik or was it elsewhere too?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: For the most part, it was up there at Grab and Tula. I mean, there was Rudina too. That is part of the Dubrovnik coast. And once I was probably in Herceg-Novi. No, not Herceg-Novi. There was some kind of exercise. I can't remember its name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Never mind. Tell me: In 1991, when the war broke out, you were 43 years old; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is still military age, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just speak up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any war assignment in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you free from your military obligation?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any mobilisation in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until the end of 1991, was there any mobilisation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't think so. I wouldn't know, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any public calls for a general mobilisation in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't say that either. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you listened to the radio during 1991 in Dubrovnik, and general mobilisation was proclaimed over the radio too, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly, because you said that during your career you drove high officials. Could you tell us briefly who it was that you drove in this period from 1970 onwards? So whose driver were you? Who did you drive?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: The presidents of the Executive Council. There were three -- four of them, until the war broke out. Do you want their names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No need for that. Tell me: Did you drive the mayor, Petar Poljanic?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. He had a different driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: When did you become the driver of the head of district of the Dubrovacko Neretvanska district?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: When it was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your line of work, could that be considered as a promotion in relation to the status of municipality and district, county?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, yes, in a way, because I imagine that the head of district or county is a higher-ranking position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Your family is from Dubrovnik, or rather, fled from Dubrovnik together with your relatives. Do you remember the period when this took place?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. Perhaps other people could remember that. Because there were these ships that were transporting our refugees. They were all examined, these ships were. They even went to Zelenika for this kind of screening. My wife and children were lucky enough not to have to go to Zelenika. They went straight to Rijeka because the Jugo wind was so strong that I imagine they didn't have a chance to screen them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I could have, but I didn't want to leave my town. My wife didn't want to leave either, but we did that for the sake of our young children. They are still traumatised until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about other men of your age? Could they leave Dubrovnik freely?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, no. Those who were able-bodied for military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If they could not because they were of military age and able-bodied, does that mean that you could not have left?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, that's not what I was saying. Perhaps I could not have left if I wanted to leave, but then I didn't want to leave in the first place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In September 1991, what were your exact duties? What was your exact position?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the month of September, in 1991, what were your exact duties? What was your exact position?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I was driver of the president of the Executive Council of the municipality of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Nikola Obuljen?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I think that he went to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is true that he went to negotiate, but that is one of the things he did. But what was he? Was he in the government or in the party structure? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: He was mayor. I mean, my mind stopped just now. He was mayor of Dubrovnik. I don't know. I'm not sure whether it was at that time or not, when Petar Poljanic was mayor exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who went to negotiate then?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I know, but I forgot. I used to know. I know that Nikola Obuljen went. I think Tonko Karaman. I don't know. I'm not sure. I don't know whether Djuro Kolic went. I don't know. I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already said that Zeljko Sikic went to the negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, I don't think that Zeljko Sikic went to negotiate. He went only once, before the war broke out, before the attack on Konavle was launched. He went to Prevlaka then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me. Tonko Karaman, in what capacity did he attend the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't really tell you about that because I didn't talk to them, and I don't know. How should I know who they talked to and what they negotiated about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Karaman?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Karaman a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, when he went to negotiate, was he a member of the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that, as a professional driver, and since you often drove high officials, you often went to the actual venues where the meetings took place? Do you talk to these officials during the drive? Do you know where they're going to? Do you have that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I do not talk about such matters while I drive, and I'm not interested in who is going where.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that contrary to the good practices and customs from the former SFRY? Drivers usually knew --

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. Everybody said that a driver could write a book, but no, that is not for us to do or say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Where did you drive Zeljko Sikic in that period, in September 1991, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: You mean September?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I only drove him around town, and towards the end -- I don't know what the exact date was, but towards the end of September, we went to Prevlaka. I don't know who he had a brief meeting with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: Do you know where Zeljko Sikic lived?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: In town. I don't know the exact address. I think it was Bana Jelacica Street. I don't know the exact house number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this outside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, outside the Old Town. I mean, that was his apartment, the apartment he had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During October, November, and December, before you were wounded, did you see him often? Did you drive him often?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I saw him every day, because he was in the building of the municipality. He didn't go anywhere, only around town, only if he'd go somewhere around town, go home and back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever drive him to his home where he slept?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever drive him from his home to his office?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No. Perhaps once, or not at all. I don't remember. He would always go on his own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those three months of 1991, October, November, and December, did you drive Zeljko Sikic at all, or any other official; and if so, how often?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we couldn't drive because it wasn't safe. We didn't have anybody to drive. I would drive for the hotel mostly, the Hotel Argentina, in fact, which is where the observers were, the monitors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you drive most often to the Hotel Argentina?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I don't know their names. There were some foreigners too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Miso Mihocevic?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive him?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, I did not. He was a translator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a liaison officer, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Liaison officer? I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Do you know somebody called Franka Babic? Actually, she was a Franciscan nun, and she was in the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Sigurate Monastery.

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Zeljko Sikic, from mid-October 1991, that is to say from mid-October 1991 to January 1992, he was in the Sigurate Monastery in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that he never told you that, as his driver, or that you ever drove him over there, or waited for him by the monastery?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: He never told me that. I don't know, nor did he drive me there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else mention that?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you that Franka Babic, the Roman Catholic nun, says that he lived at the Sigurate Monastery during that period of time, what would you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, what could I say?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that possible or not?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you anything. I don't know. I can't tell you anything about other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Zeljko Sikic well?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know him that well, but of course I know him. I was his chauffeur.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you on good terms with him?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: Yes, I am. But he never told me that. I just went to his apartment to Ban Jelacic once. I don't know the number, but he had an apartment there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did his family stay on in Dubrovnik or did they leave Dubrovnik like your own family did?

utterances.speaker: MATO VALJALO
utterances.text: I think -- I'm not quite sure, but I think his family left later too. His wife. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is it time to break? Is my time up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic. We will resume, then, on Monday. I'm afraid I must ask you to return on Monday to continue your evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 9th day of February 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
